programme.json.summary: In The Open Group's ArchiSurance case study the company was formed by merging three insurers, one per product line. Each kept its own back office and systems. This illustrative programme moves home, travel, car and legal aid onto shared customer, policy and claims components, following the Component and One Stop principles in the Archi model.

decisions.title: Single policy administration platform
decisions.options: Extend the Home & Away platform to all lines · Buy a new policy administration package · Keep separate systems behind a shared customer layer
decisions.hypothesis: Extend Home & Away. It already holds the shared customer and policy components named in the Archi model. Widest blast radius in the estate, and it runs on the mainframe.

decisions.title: One CRM and contact centre platform
decisions.options: Replace both with one SaaS platform · Keep the CRM, replace the call centre application
decisions.hypothesis: Replace the agent desktop first, then decide on the CRM once the single customer view is live.

decisions.title: Mainframe future
decisions.options: Retain and modernise · Rehost on standard platforms · Retire together with a policy administration replacement
decisions.hypothesis: Retain through the consolidation; decide after the policy platform decision, because it sets most of the mainframe workload.

decisions.title: Claims platform
decisions.options: Claims workflow on top of Claim Data Management · Full claims system replacement
decisions.hypothesis: Grow the claims workflow and shrink Claim Data Management to a record store.

decisions.title: Shared document processing
decisions.options: Keep the Document Processing SSC tools · Move to a digital mailroom service
decisions.hypothesis: Digital mailroom; the SSC already serves all lines.

taxonomy.definition: A customer-facing outcome ArchiSurance organises itself around.
An end-to-end customer or business journey inside a value stream, from trigger to outcome.
One activity in a journey. Carries RACI, the applications used and the capabilities it realises.
The top tier of the process hierarchy: Operate (serves customers), Manage (directs and controls), Support (keeps the insurer running).
A group of related processes, aligned to APQC PCF (insurance).
A repeatable business process with an owner, applications and capabilities. Operate processes link to journeys.
A broad area of what the insurer does, independent of organisation and systems.
A specific ability the insurer needs, aligned to an ACORD-style insurance capability model. Stable over time even when processes and systems change.
A specific ability inside an L2 capability, mapped to the applications that realise it; an L3 with no application is a gap.
A large piece of change that serves one or more strategic initiatives, regulatory requirements or consolidation decision, delivered as several features.

A deliverable change with a target quarter and status. Its footprint names the applications it changes and how (new, enhance, configure, integrate, replace, retire), the L3 capabilities and the journey steps whose way of working changes. The atlas traces its impact from that footprint.
A job role or external party that performs process steps. Linked through RACI.
A software system or service the insurer uses or depends on, including platforms and partner-hosted services.
An application other applications run on. Linked through 'runs on' with a status.
A data flow from one application to another, with its data, integration type and frequency.
A business data subject with one system of record and several consumers.
A physical site that hosts ArchiSurance workloads.
A third party that provides software, services, hosting or a partnership.
The master agreement with a supplier: term, notice, renewal and key clauses.
The licence or subscription for one application: model, metric, entitlement, usage and cost.
How one application is supported: resolver groups, hours, SLAs and vendor end of support.
One of ArchiSurance's strategic priorities or goals.
A strategic achievement or programme under a pillar, traced to the journeys, processes, capabilities and applications it depends on.
A modelled disruption, change or regulation, with the items it affects. The impact is computed from the repository, so it stays current as the data changes.
One obligation from a regulation, mapped to the applications, capabilities and processes that must change.
A key platform decision raised by the consolidation programme, with options, an EA hypothesis, a phase and a blast radius.
A stated position or commitment, paraphrased, with its architecture implication.

glossary.definition: A gap is a capability with no supporting application. Overlap is a capability served by three or more applications.
Tier 0: the organisation cannot operate without it. Tier 1: major customer or regulatory impact. Tier 2: significant internal impact. Tier 3: low impact.
How far a record can be trusted. Customer-provided: confirmed by the organisation. Public: from a public source. Partly confirmed: capability confirmed, product assumed. Illustrative: placeholder.
Business-built tools such as spreadsheets and desktop databases. They carry control risk when used for critical processes.
How well an application meets business needs, scored 1 to 5.
Where an application is in its life: Production, Migrating, Phase-out.
Annual licence plus support cost for an application. Illustrative until supplied.
Gartner model for portfolio decisions. Tolerate: keep, minimal spend. Invest: strategic, develop further. Migrate: valuable function on weak technology, move it. Eliminate: retire.
How sound an application's technology is (supportability, currency, resilience), scored 1 to 5.
APQC Process Classification Framework. A widely used process taxonomy with cross-industry and industry editions.
The Open Group modelling language for enterprise architecture. Models from tools such as Archi can be imported into the atlas.
Everything affected if an application or decision changes: value streams, journeys, capabilities, interfaces and cost.
What the organisation must be able to do, described independently of who does it or which system supports it.
How work is done: a repeatable set of steps with an owner, inputs and outputs.
The practice of describing how the organisation's business, data, applications and technology fit together, so change can be planned and its impact understood.
A point in a process map where work passes from one role to another. More handoffs usually mean more delay and more risk of error.
An end-to-end path a customer or colleague follows within a value stream, from a trigger to an outcome.
The set of element types and the relationships allowed between them. It is the structure behind this repository.
The three tiers of the process hierarchy. Operate serves customers, Manage directs and controls the organisation, Support keeps it running.
A diagram of a journey where each lane is a role, boxes are steps in sequence, and a systems lane shows the applications used.
Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the outcome, one per step), Consulted (gives input), Informed (kept up to date).
One of the organisation's strategic priorities or goals, under which initiatives are grouped.

Whether the applications a strategic initiative depends on are rated to support it. An initiative is flagged Watch when a Tier 0 or Tier 1 application behind it is rated Migrate or Eliminate, or scores below 3 for technical health.
The application that holds the authoritative version of a data domain.
The Open Group Architecture Framework. A method for developing and governing enterprise architecture.
The agreed hierarchy and names for each element type, so the same thing is always described the same way.
The ability to follow links from a role to its steps, capabilities, applications and suppliers, and back again.
A sequence of activities that delivers an outcome a customer values.
Several features changing the same application within one quarter, competing for release slots, environments and testing.
What a feature changes: applications with a change type, L3 capabilities, journey steps, drivers and dependencies. The impact is derived from it.

How far a feature or epic reaches across the organisation: applications changed and their criticality, integrations to rework or retest, journeys, people to retrain, critical services, customer exposure and new integrations. Rated Low, Medium, High or Critical.
Building on an application that a programme decision may replace or converge soon after, so the work may have to be redone.
Retesting a connected application whose interface is unchanged, to confirm a change elsewhere has not broken it.
A contract term that gives the supplier rights (for example to terminate or renegotiate) when the customer's ownership changes.
The date after which the vendor stops fixes and security patches for a version.
A documented and ideally tested plan to leave a supplier without disrupting service.
What a licence is charged on: named users, cores, processors, policies, accounts, transactions or capacity.
The last date to serve notice before a contract renews or ends: the term end minus the notice period.
Usage above licence entitlement. A compliance and audit exposure.
Systems integrator (builds and changes systems) and application management services (runs and supports them).
Service level agreement. Here: availability target and P1 response and resolution times.
Software as a service. The vendor hosts and runs the application; the customer subscribes.
Licences paid for but not used. Flagged here when utilisation is below 65%.
How up to date a deployed version is: Current, N-1 (one behind), N-2 or older.
A price comparison website that collects quotes from several insurers.
A periodic report of policies or claims written under delegated authority.
Loss ratio plus expense ratio. Below 100% means an underwriting profit.
An arrangement where a coverholder or managing general agent underwrites or settles claims on the insurer's behalf.
The first report of a claim, when the basic facts are captured.
Incurred but not reported: claims for events that have happened but have not yet been notified.
The person or property covered by the policy. Often the policyholder, but not always.
A firm that arranges insurance on behalf of customers and is paid commission or fees.
A policy that ends because the premium was not paid or the customer did not renew.
Cover for the cost of legal advice and action, also called legal aid insurance in some markets.
An independent expert who investigates and values a claim for the insurer.
Claims incurred divided by premiums earned.
A change to a policy during its term, such as a new address or added cover.
The person or organisation that owns the insurance contract and pays the premium.
The price paid for cover, usually annually or in instalments.
A characteristic used to price a risk, such as age, location or claims history.
Insurance bought by an insurer to transfer part of its risk. Treaty covers a portfolio; facultative covers one risk.
Offering and agreeing cover for a further term.
Money set aside for claims that have been reported but not yet paid (case reserve) or not yet reported (IBNR).
The insurer's right to recover a claim payment from the party responsible for the loss.
Deciding whether to accept a risk and on what terms and price.
The control point for APIs: security, throttling and routing.
Change data capture. Streams changes from a database as events.
A platform that runs applications in containers and manages them automatically.
A platform for publishing and consuming streams of events in real time, such as Apache Kafka.
Governance, risk and compliance tooling: risk registers, controls and policies.
Identity and access management, and privileged access management for administrator accounts.
IT service management (incident, change, problem) and the configuration management database.
A large central computer for high-volume transaction processing.
Middleware for reliable system-to-system messaging, such as IBM MQ or RabbitMQ.
Security information and event management, and the security operations centre that uses it.
Software that runs many virtual servers on shared hardware.
A fictional insurer used by The Open Group and the Archi tool to illustrate ArchiMate. This atlas is built from the Archi sample model.
The payment network in the Archi model that connects ArchiSurance's Bank System with customers' banks.
ArchiSurance's shared service centre that turns paper claim forms and contracts into electronic documents.
The business interface intermediaries use to reach ArchiSurance in the Archi model, shown here as the Intermediary Portal.
Day 1 is the legal or operational start of a programme such as completion of a merger. Waves are later phases.
EA hypothesis for each application under a major programme such as a merger, acquisition or transformation. Typical values: Retain, Assess, Likely converge, Key decision, Replace / decommission.
Cost saved by combining operations, systems or suppliers.
A function whose disruption would materially impair the insurer's performance, compliance or continuity. Used by DORA and by Solvency II outsourcing rules.

EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, applying since 17 January 2025. Covers ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and ICT third-party risk for insurers and other financial entities.
The DORA article listing the key contract terms required for ICT services, such as service descriptions, locations, audit rights and exit.

EU regulation on artificial intelligence. AI used for risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance is high-risk. A provisional agreement in 2026 moved stand-alone high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 (to confirm).
EU General Data Protection Regulation. Rules on processing personal data, including lawful basis, data subject rights, breach notification and records of processing.
EU Insurance Distribution Directive: rules on how insurance is sold, including demands and needs, product oversight and governance, and conflicts of interest.
The accounting standard for insurance contracts, effective from January 2023.
International standard for information security management systems.
EU Network and Information Security Directive 2. Cyber risk management and incident reporting duties for essential and important entities.
Own risk and solvency assessment: the insurer's own view of its risks and capital needs.
Under Solvency II, outsourcing a critical or important function needs prior notification to the supervisor and stronger contract terms and oversight.
IDD rules requiring insurers to design, approve and review products for a defined target market.
Solvency II reporting: quantitative reporting templates, the public solvency and financial condition report, and the regular supervisory report.
The DORA register of all ICT third-party arrangements that each financial entity must keep and report.
Solvency capital requirement and minimum capital requirement under Solvency II.
EU prudential framework for insurers: capital requirements (Pillar 1), governance and risk management including ORSA (Pillar 2), and reporting and disclosure (Pillar 3).

Amendments to the Solvency II Directive published in January 2025, applying at the latest from 30 January 2027. Changes cover proportionality, Pillar 1 calibration, macroprudential tools, sustainability risks and reporting.
Both sites run live at the same time and share load.
One site runs live while the other is on standby and takes over only after a failover.
A disaster recovery exercise that proves a service can be recovered within its RTO and RPO.
The maximum tolerable disruption to an important business service.
Recovery point objective. The maximum data loss allowed, measured as time before the failure.
Recovery time objective. The maximum time a service may be down before it must be restored.
Moving live service from the primary site to the secondary after a failure or for a test.
An application that keeps running but loses its fallback, such as its standby site or hosting.
Small, Medium, Large or Very large. The impact level for change and regulatory scenarios, which are planned rather than disruptive.

programme.name: Back-office consolidation
programme.summary: In The Open Group's ArchiSurance case study the company was formed by merging three insurers, one per product line. Each kept its own back office and systems. This illustrative programme moves home, travel, car and legal aid onto shared customer, policy and claims components, following the Component and One Stop principles in the Archi model.
programme.view_sub: What the consolidation means for the architecture: programme principles, the addressable run cost, contract exposure and the key platform decisions.

milestones.label: Car policies migrated to the Home & Away platform
Legacy car and legal aid systems retired

phase_notes.Phase 1 (2026-27): Plus: programme governance, data migration approach, product mapping between lines.

decisions.title: Single policy administration platform
decisions.options: Extend the Home & Away platform to all lines · Buy a new policy administration package · Keep separate systems behind a shared customer layer
decisions.hypothesis: Extend Home & Away. It already holds the shared customer and policy components named in the Archi model. Widest blast radius in the estate, and it runs on the mainframe.

decisions.title: One CRM and contact centre platform
decisions.options: Replace both with one SaaS platform · Keep the CRM, replace the call centre application
decisions.hypothesis: Replace the agent desktop first, then decide on the CRM once the single customer view is live.

decisions.title: Mainframe future
decisions.options: Retain and modernise · Rehost on standard platforms · Retire together with a policy administration replacement
decisions.hypothesis: Retain through the consolidation; decide after the policy platform decision, because it sets most of the mainframe workload.

decisions.title: Claims platform
decisions.options: Claims workflow on top of Claim Data Management · Full claims system replacement
decisions.hypothesis: Grow the claims workflow and shrink Claim Data Management to a record store.

decisions.title: Shared document processing
decisions.options: Keep the Document Processing SSC tools · Move to a digital mailroom service
decisions.hypothesis: Digital mailroom; the SSC already serves all lines.

commitments.stated: Customers have one point of contact for all products and claims.
commitments.implication: Shared customer data and one contact centre platform; product-line systems must feed the CRM.

commitments.stated: Product lines share application components instead of running their own.
commitments.implication: Car and legal aid move to the shared policy and customer components; legacy systems retire.

commitments.stated: Applications run on a small set of standard platforms.
commitments.implication: Mainframe and Unix farm consolidate; new workloads go to cloud.

commitments.stated: Fewer products and vendors, licensed for real use.
commitments.implication: Retiring the legacy systems removes two vendors and their support contracts.
